title: Japan's Teachers Struggling with Workloads
paragraphs: Teachers in Japan are overworked, struggling with excessive duties, and dealing with emotional exhaustion, according to a new survey.
The findings also show a major gap between working targets set by the government and the daily realities in Japanese schools.
Publishing company Shogakukan surveyed almost 2,700 education professionals between May and July this year.

By law, teachers should work no more than 8 hours a day, but according to the survey results, teachers are actually working an average of 11 hours per day, with 79% working at least 10 hours, and 24% working over 12 hours each day.
By law, teachers should also get at least 60 minutes of break time a day, but the results show that just 0.2% of teachers are getting this. In fact, 65% said they took no breaks at all.
Many teachers also said having to take work home is normal. Fifty percent said they take work home three or more days a week, while 86% said they have to work on their days off.
In 2025, the government set targets to reduce teachers' overtime hours. However, teachers say this has resulted in pressure to hide their real overtime hours.

One teacher said it was frustrating to be told to leave work early, even though they hadn't finished their tasks. Another said that teachers felt they either had to take work home so it wouldn't be counted as overtime, or change their time cards to hide the real hours they were working.
In fact, rather than cutting overtime hours, 61% said they would rather have their emotional exhaustion reduced.
Despite these problems, 68% said they wouldn't quit teaching because they found happiness in children's smiles, their growth and their achievements.
